models.collectorNote: About 2,450 built. The Roadster proved an EV could be a sports car at all, and its historical position keeps values strong — battery health and documentation matter more than mileage.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: A Lotus Elise chassis with the body restyled and the powertrain replaced. 0–60 mph in under four seconds in Sport trim, at a time when the industry still treated EVs as compliance homework.

models.intro: The car that started it. Tesla's first product took a Lotus Elise chassis, replaced the running gear with batteries and a single electric motor, and proved in 2008 that an electric car could be the fast one. A successor has been promised for years and has not reached production.
models.name: Roadster

generations.name: Original design
generations.note: The sedan that made the industry take Tesla seriously: 265 miles of EPA range in top form and a 17-inch touchscreen in place of a dashboard. Performance versions got quicker every year.

generations.name: Facelift and Plaid
generations.note: The 2016 facelift dropped the black nose cone; the 2021 overhaul brought the tri-motor Plaid — 1,020 hp and a claimed 0–60 mph time under two seconds with rollout, the quickest production sedan ever tested.

models.intro: The car that forced every major maker to build an EV program. Launched in 2012 with range and acceleration no production EV had combined before, and still on sale — heavily revised underneath — more than a decade later.
models.name: Model S

generations.name: Original design
generations.note: A dashboard reduced to one 15-inch screen and almost no buttons — copied across the industry within five years. Production hell in 2017–2018 nearly broke the company; the car that came out the other side changed the market anyway.

generations.name: Facelift (Highland)
generations.note: Quieter cabin, better materials, indicators moved to buttons on the wheel — the controversial part. The Performance version makes 510 hp and is the one keen drivers should stretch for.

models.intro: Tesla's mass-market bet, and the car that took EVs mainstream: over two million sold, the best-selling EV in the world for stretches of its life, and the reason every legacy maker now has an electric sedan program.
models.name: Model 3

generations.name: Original design
generations.note: Effectively a taller Model 3 with a hatch, sharing most of its parts — and it outsold the sedan by a wide margin. In 2023 it became the best-selling car in the world of any powertrain, the first EV to hold that title.

generations.name: Facelift (Juniper)
generations.note: Full-width light bars, a quieter and better-finished cabin, and the indicator stalk restored after the Model 3 experiment. Same formula underneath — it didn't need changing.

models.intro: The best-selling car in the world in 2023 — not the best-selling EV, the best-selling car, full stop. The Model Y is the Model 3's formula raised onto a crossover body, and it outsells everything Tesla makes combined.
models.name: Model Y

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Stainless-steel exoskeleton panels that can't be stamped the normal way, steer-by-wire with no mechanical backup, and a 48-volt electrical architecture the rest of the industry is now studying. The Cyberbeast tri-motor version makes 845 hp.

models.intro: Unveiled in 2019 with a smashed window on stage, delivered from late 2023. The Cybertruck's stainless wedge looks like a rendering error; underneath sit genuinely radical choices — steer-by-wire and a 48V architecture — wrapped in the most polarising truck ever sold.
models.name: Cybertruck
